# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXII. Nell Is Invited Out to Tea

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“AND what makes your eyes bulge like that. Now?” Thirza inquired, as Nell returned from a quick trip to the post office. “Have you found another like-minded soul?” Excitement draped over Nell like a dress, gleamed in her eyes, and illuminated all her features. Through the warm sunlight and drifting shadows of the August dusk, she had come skipping up the lane, resembling a gust-driven fairy.
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0000 }

“No, Thirza, but oh, what do you think? Tomorrow afternoon, I have been invited to the manse for tea! At the post office, Mrs. Wace dropped off the letter for me. Thirza, just look at it. ‘Miss Nell Harcourt, Grey Shutters.’ Never before was I referred to as ‘Miss.’ It gave me such a thrill! Among my choicest treasures, I shall forever cherish it.”
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0001 }

“Mrs. Wace mentioned that her intention was to invite every child in her Sunday-school class for tea one by one,” Thirza remarked, viewing the extraordinary occurrence with great composure. “There is no need for you to become so agitated about it. My dear, you must try to accept events with tranquility.”
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0002 }

Had Nell reacted with composure, it would have required an alteration of her very character. Being entirely “spirit and fire and dew,” both the joys and the sorrows of living struck her with a threefold force. Recognizing this, Thirza experienced a subtle anxiety, aware that life's fluctuations would likely fall heavily upon such a spontaneous spirit, yet failing to fully comprehend that an equivalent aptitude for joy could overcompensate. Consequently, Thirza believed it her responsibility to train Nell into a serene evenness of temperament that was as unachievable and foreign to her as to a sunbeam dancing in a shallow brook. As she regretfully conceded to herself, she was not achieving much progress. Whenever a cherished expectation or scheme failed, Nell was cast into “deeps of affliction.” Whenever it was realized, she was elevated to dizzying heights of joy. Thirza was nearly losing hope of ever transforming this global stray into her ideal modest child possessed of reserved behavior and stiff decorum. Nor would she have accepted that she actually preferred Nell far more precisely as she was.
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0003 }

Overcome with silent grief, Nell retired for the night since Obed had mentioned the wind coming from the northeast, making him worry that rain would fall the following day. Hearing the poplar trees rustle around the dwelling distressed her, as it resembled the tapping of rain, while the distant, deep bellow of the gulf—a sound she usually enjoyed for its unusual, resonant, and persistent beat—now felt like a forewarning of tempests and ruin to a young girl who desperately desired pleasant weather. It seemed to Nell that dawn would be delayed forever.
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0004 }

However, every single thing eventually concludes, even those nights preceding the date you are asked for tea at the manse. Regardless of what Obed had predicted, the morning turned out beautiful, causing Nell’s mood to reach its ultimate peak. Washing the dishes from breakfast, she cried out, “Oh, Thirza, a feeling inside me today makes me simply adore all the people I lay eyes on! My feelings are so wonderful, you cannot imagine! If only it might endure, wouldn't that be lovely? Were I merely asked to tea each day, I think I could become an exemplary child. Yet, Thirza, oh, a serious nature belongs to this event as well. Nervousness fills me so. Suppose my manners fail to be correct? As you are aware, taking tea at a manse has never happened to me previously, and despite my reading of the guidelines provided inside the Family Herald’s Etiquette Department from the moment I arrived here, my knowledge of all etiquette rules remains uncertain. Doing something foolish or failing to perform a required act frightens me greatly. If a person desired something immensely, would accepting another portion align with polite behavior?”
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0005 }

“Your problem, Nell, is that your own self occupies too much of your thoughts. Your focus ought to be simply on Mrs. Wace and whatever she would find pleasant and delightful,” declared Thirza, who, for a single moment in her existence, struck upon a most sensible and concise bit of counsel. Nell grasped the truth of this right away.
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0006 }

“Thirza, you are correct. I will attempt to refrain from giving any thought to myself.”
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0007 }

It was clear that Nell had managed her call without committing any grave faux pas, as she returned in the evening dusk beneath a vast, lofty sky adorned with streaks of rose and yellow clouds, her spirits completely elevated; she sat upon the large red-sandstone step by the kitchen doorway, resting her weary, curly head upon Thirza’s gingham apron, and joyfully recounted the entire experience to Thirza.
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0008 }

Down over the extensive harvest fields, a chill breeze swept from the edges of fir-covered western hills and blew loudly through the poplars. Above the orchard, a single bright star was suspended, and across Linger Lane, fireflies darted back and forth amid the ferns and swaying branches. As she spoke, Nell observed them, feeling in some way that the breeze, stars, and fireflies had all become intertwined into an indescribably lovely and magical thing.
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0009 }

“Oh, Thirza, my time was exceedingly fascinating. I believe my life has not been in vain, a feeling I will retain forever even if another invitation to tea at a manse is never extended to me. Upon my arrival, Mrs. Wace greeted me at the entrance. The most charming pale-pink organdy dress clothed her, complete with many frills and sleeves reaching her elbows, making her look precisely like a seraph. Truly, Thirza, I think being a minister's wife when I mature would suit me. Because a minister would not focus on such earthly matters, my red hair might not bother him. Naturally, however, a person would need to be inherently good for that, which I will never achieve, so considering it is likely pointless. Certain individuals possess natural goodness, as you know, while others do not. I belong among the others. Mrs. Sowerby claims that original sin fills me. Regardless of how diligently I attempt to be good, I can never succeed to the extent of those possessing natural goodness. It resembles geometry quite a bit, I imagine. Nevertheless, don't you believe that trying so intensely should be worth something? Belonging to those who are naturally good, Mrs. Wace is someone I love passionately. As you know, certain people, such as Obed and Mrs. Wace, can be loved instantly without any effort. Conversely, loving others, such as Mrs. Sowerby, requires immense effort. Since they possess great knowledge and work so actively in the church, you realize you should love them, yet unless you continuously remind yourself, you forget. Originating from the Pale Sands Sunday-school, another little girl attended tea at the manse. Laurette Bradley was her name, and she proved to be a very pleasant little girl. Although not precisely a soulmate, you understand, she was nevertheless very pleasant. Our tea was splendid, and I believe I observed all the decorum rules fairly well. Following tea, Mrs. Wace performed music and sang, and she persuaded Lauretta and me to join in singing as well. Mrs. Wace remarks that my voice is good and states that I must perform in the Sunday-school choir from now on. The pure idea thrilled me beyond what you can imagine. Singing in the Sunday-school choir, just as Isolde does, has been a deep desire of mine, though I worried it was a privilege beyond my reach. Due to a major concert occurring at the Pale Sands Hotel this evening where her sister will recite, Lauretta had to depart early. According to Lauretta, the Americans residing at the hotel organize a concert every two weeks to benefit the Port Marlow hospital, and they request many individuals from Pale Sands to recite. Lauretta mentioned that she anticipates being invited herself eventually. I merely stared at her with reverence. Following her departure, Mrs. Wace and I shared an intimate conversation. I revealed all to her—concerning Mrs. Thomas, the twins, Lettie Marchant, Melisande, my arrival at Grey Shutters, and my struggles with geometry. Can you imagine it, Thirza? Mrs. Wace confessed to me that she too was a fool when it came to geometry. That heartened me immensely. Just prior to my departure, Mrs. Sowerby arrived at the manse, and what do you suppose, Thirza? A new teacher has been hired by the trustees, and she is a woman. Miss Agnes Thorne is her name. Is that not an enchanting name? According to Mrs. Sowerby, a female teacher has never been employed in Brierley previously, and she regards it as a perilous change. Yet I feel having a woman as a teacher will be wonderful, and I truly do not know how I will endure the fortnight remaining until school opens. Seeing her makes me so eager.”
{: #nw-v01-c22-p0010 }
